Series::airy¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::airy() const

The Airy Ai Transform¶

airy() evaluates the Airy function Ai elementwise. Ai is the particular solution of y''(x) - x y(x) = 0 that decays toward zero on the positive real axis. This combination of an oscillating negative half-line and a rapidly decaying positive half-line makes Ai useful around turning points, where a differential equation changes from oscillatory to exponential behavior.

The method computes Ai, not its independent companion Bi. Three facts help identify the result: Ai(0) = 0.3550280538...; Ai oscillates for negative arguments; and it remains positive while decaying exponentially for positive arguments.

This is an out-of-place, elementwise transform. It preserves rank, shape, and platform. Floating input is evaluated at its floating precision; integral and boolean input is promoted to float64, because Ai is not integer-valued. Complex input is not part of the real-valued contract.

The central interval is evaluated from the convergent solution of the Airy differential equation. The tails use asymptotic forms so large arguments do not force badly conditioned power-series cancellation. Positive arguments beyond the representable exponential tail approach exact 0.0. Infinite real input returns NaN; no finite oscillatory value exists at infinity.

Reverse Mode¶

airy() records a unary reverse node. If a = x.airy(), then da/dx = Ai'(x), so an incoming sensitivity is multiplied elementwise by Ai'(x). Shape is unchanged and no broadcast reduction is required. The derivative at zero is Ai'(0) = -0.2588194038....

Examples¶

Example 1. Values on both sides of the turning point show the oscillatory and decaying regimes.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).airy());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0.2274, 0.5356, 0.3550, 0.1353, 0.0349]

Example 2. The transform is lane-wise. A matrix remains a matrix, and integer storage is promoted before evaluation.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({{-1, 0}, {1, 2}}).airy());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 0.5356 0.3550 ⎤
⎣ 0.1353 0.0349 ⎦

Example 3. Summing seeds every output lane with one, so the stored sensitivity is Ai' at each input lane.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.airy().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.0102, -0.2588, -0.1591]

Example 4. Scalar rank is preserved; a scalar does not become a one-element vector.

const auto a = pluss::make_series(0.0).airy();
std::cout << "dim=" << a.dim() << " value=" << a.item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

dim=0 value=0.355028

See Also¶

  • besselj() is another oscillatory special function.

  • erf() is an elementwise integral-defined special function.

  • reverse() seeds and propagates sensitivities.
